col4_Comment:
Food Insecure
We have used a UK wide figure as figures specific to Nottingham are not available.

The proportion of food secure households decreased from 92% in 2019 to 2020, to 90% in 2023 to 2024, a decrease of two percentage points. The proportion of food secure households remained the same between 2022 to 2023 and 2023 to 2024.
The majority of households were food secure, with high household food security (83%) or marginal household food security (6%). Food insecure households were in the minority, with low household food security (5%) or very low household food security (5%).
Source: Family Resources Survey: financial year 2023 to 2024 - GOV.UK

Food Desert
We have used the percentage of residential properties not within 1 mile to estimate the percentage population as figures per resident were not available.

We have utilised a dataset of supermarkets produced by a company called Geolytix (https://geolytix.com/blog/supermarket-retail-points/). They classify supermarkets into local, small, medium and large by floor space. For the purpose of this work we have excluded those classified as local (<280m sq) as these would be considered 'convenience stores' often with higher pricing. The data does not include independents.

We used road and path network analysis to determine the percentage of residential properties that are not within 1 mile of a supermarket, as this better represents accessibility than an 'as the crow flies' analysis.

This gave 3,677 out of 144,209 residential properties - 2.5% of Nottingham's residential properties.

col4_Comment:
As part of the Ask Cardiff 2024 survey, residents were asked whether in the last six months, they or anyone else in their household had skipped meals because they couldn't afford food. Results were broadly similar to the findings of the 2023 survey, with around one in 6 (15.9%) eating smaller meals than usual, or skipping meals because they couldn't afford food; one in twelve (8.6%) missed meals to afford to pay bills. The proportion of respondents receiving food from a food bank or charity increased from 2.5% in 2023 to 4.4%.

Respondents under the age of 35 were most likely to have undertaken at least one of the options listed (38.5%), followed by those identifying as disabled (31.0%), and residents of the Southern Arc (30.3%). Respondents over the age of 55 were most likely to report they had done 'none' of the options listed (86.6%). Around one in fourteen of those identifying as disabled (7.7%) reported that they had 'not eaten for a whole day' - the highest proportion of all demographic groups analysed, reflecting the findings of the previous year.

There was a broad correlation with those unable to afford food and the level of deprivation. As in previous years, respondents living in the most deprived areas of the city were notably more likely to report having been impacted by not being able to afford food, with 29.3% 'eating smaller meals, or skipping meals' completely; a fifth (20.0%) 'missed meals to be able to pay bills'; almost one in seven (12.9%) had 'been hungry but not eaten'. 

The proportion of those in the most deprived areas reporting they had not 'eaten for a whole day' (9.8%) or 'received food from a food bank or charity' (12.0%) increased from 6.3% and 4.5% respectively in 2023.

The NHSGGC Adult Health and Wellbeing Survey also use questions from the FIES. 

Restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic increased levels of food insecurity due to difficulties in accessing food, as well as being able to afford enough food. Glasgow City Food Plan is a 10-year framework to achieve “a food system in Glasgow that is fair, resilient and environmentally sustainable and enables everyone in Glasgow to eat healthy, affordable, culturally appropriate Good Food irrespective of where they live, their income or personal circumstances”. Based around 3 overarching pillars, Equity, Sustainability and Health, 2 of the 6 themes of the plan are 'Food poverty - fair food for all' and 'Children and young people'. A long-term outcome of the Glasgow Food Plan is 'improved access to healthy affordable food and reduced food insecurity'. Partnership work to tackle food insecurity has been strengthened and increased focus is placed on maximising household income, promoting “cash first” approaches and testing and developing new models of support. http://goodfoodforall.co.uk/home/glasgow-city-food-plan

col4_Comment: According to proxy data derived from Turkish Statistical Institute (TURKSTAT) income and poverty reports, and aligned with FAO's Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES), it is estimated that approximately 7% of Ankara's population experiences moderate or severe food insecurity. This group faces difficulties in accessing nutritionally adequate and safe food due to rising food prices, inflation, and limited household income. Vulnerable groups include low-income households, refugees, and unemployed individuals, who often rely on municipal social assistance programs, food banks, or subsidized markets provided by Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (AMM). While no official data exists on “food deserts” in Ankara, preliminary observations suggest that physical access to supermarkets and fresh food markets is relatively widespread in central districts due to the presence of municipal “halk pazarları” (public markets) and grocery stores. However, peri-urban and low-income settlements on the city's outskirts may face challenges in affordable and continuous access to fresh food. Further mapping and collaboration with universities and FAO are required to quantify food desert prevalence using internationally comparable methodologies such as the USDA definition. In the absence of standardized local data, AMM acknowledges the gap and plans to prioritize monitoring systems for food environment and nutrition security within the framework of SDG2.

To note: the figure reported here is not an official City of Cape Town statistic, but is based on the below mentioned studies in the absence of official reported figures. Since 2009, the Statistics South Africa General Household Survey (GHS) has also included a set of 8 questions based on the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale to determine household food security. The following index was used;

Households that answered yes to:
•max one question are considered food secure
•2-5 questions are considered food insecure
•6-8 questions are considered severely food insecure.

The results of the 2024 GHS categorizes 13.5% of households in Cape Town as being food insecure, while 9.1% was found to be severely food insecure. Thus, a total of 22.6%.

The City has recently committed to conducting socio-economic surveys every two years to obtain accurate, reliable, frequent and updated data on households across the city. Hunger-related questions were included in the CCT Household Survey, which were taken verbatim from the GHS; including:
In the last 12 months:
-did any adult (18 years and older) in this household go hungry because there wasn't enough food?
-did any child (17 years and younger) in this household go hungry because there wasn't enough food?

The CCT Household Survey took place in. 2024 and interviews with 10 000 households revealed:
•16.5% of adults in Cape Town households seldom or sometimes went hungry because there wasn't enough food, while 2% often or always went hungry due to food shortages.
•13.9% of adults in Cape Town households seldom or sometimes went hungry because there wasn't enough food, while 1.7% often or always went hungry due to food shortages.
•There are more than double the number of households with child and adult hunger in informal and backyard dwellings compared to formal dwellings.

Other previous research: 
•The National Food and Nutrition Security Report for South Africa 2024 presented the findings, at a provincial level, of a national household food security survey conducted in 2023. Based on the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale approach, 45% of households were food secure, 37% reported mild/moderate food insecurity, while 17% of households reported severe food insecurity. 
•Cape Town City Food Systems Report by AfriFOODlinks (2024) https://afrifoodlinks.org/resource/state-of-the-city-food-system-cape-town/

Food Insecure:

The Commerce Commission's website, noted that approximately 15-20% of New Zealand's population is 'food insecure.' Meanwhile, the World Bank estimated that 15.1% of New Zealanders experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2021.

Source 1: https://comcom.govt.nz/__data/assets/pdf_file/0030/265809/Kore-Hiakai-Zero-Hunger-Collective-Submission-on-Market-study-into-grocery-sector-draft-report-26-August-2021.pdf

Source 2: https://databank.worldbank.org/source/world-development-indicators#

Food Desert:

We estimated the number of people living in food deserts in Wellington City using the following method:

We have gathered a set of GIS layers from various sources to conduct our analysis. First, we accessed the GeoHealth Laboratory work programme data, which includes research on the spatial distribution and accessibility of amenities across New Zealand. For our analysis, we focused on mesh blocks where the network distance to the following amenities exceeds 1 mile (1,609 meters):
•     Closest fast-food outlet
•     Closest takeaway
•     Closest dairy/convenience store
•     Closest fruit and vegetable store
•     Closest supermarket

To estimate the population within these food desert areas, we included data from the Census at the SA1 level. By overlaying these two datasets, we estimated the total number of people residing in food desert areas. According to the in 2023 census, the number of people residing in food dessert area is: 10542 people. Given 2023 Wellington City's population of 209905, this accounts for 5.02% of the population living in food dessert. A food desert map has been uploaded in section 11.1 (Further Information).

Esto significa que más de 4.3 millones de menores en Argentina sufrieron problemas para acceder a una alimentación adecuada. El estudio señala que la inseguridad alimentaria en la infancia es un problema estructural agravado por los factores de pobreza, precariedad laboral y desempleo que afectan a Argentina hace décadas, atravesado por una serie de crisis económicas recurrentes. https://uca.edu.ar/es/noticias/inseguridad-alimentaria-en-la-infancia-argentina-un-problema-estructural-observado-en-la-coyuntura-actual-1\n

Sin embargo, no existe un porcentaje oficial específico de la población del municipio que viva en un 'desierto alimentario' (definido por la falta de acceso físico a tiendas de alimentos frescos y asequibles). Las cifras disponibles se refieren principalmente a la carencia por acceso a la alimentación nutritiva, una medida de pobreza multidimensional utilizada por el Consejo Nacional de Evaluación de la Política de Desarrollo Social (CONEVAL). 

A nivel estatal, cerca del 9.7% al 10% de la población padece algún grado de pobreza o carencia alimentaria, lo que representa a unas 384,900 personas en todo el estado, según datos de 2024.

Para porcentaje de la población que vive un desierto alimentario.
La marginación se asocia a la carencia de oportunidades sociales y a la ausencia de capacidades para adquirirlas o generarlas, a la inaccesibilidad de bienes y servicios fundamentales para el bienestar. 
El Consejo Nacional de Población evalúa el grado de marginación social a través de cuatro variables utilizadas para la determinación de las zonas son: educación (escasa o nula escolaridad), vivienda (ausencia de servicios como agua entubada que perjudica la salud y potencia la presencia de enfermedades gastrointestinales), distribución de la población, e ingresos (personas con ingresos de menos de dos salarios mínimos para adquisición de bienes, alimentos y servicios). CONAPO estratifica 5 niveles de marginación (de muy bajo a muy alto).
Para Saltillo con estimaciones de la CONAPO con base en el Censo Nacional de Población y Vivienda del Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (INEGI), con periodicidad del 2020, de las 863,574 personas habitantes en el municipio de Saltillo, 4,156 de acuerdo con el cálculo, se encuentran en alto y muy alto grado de marginación social, es decir, el 0.48%.

question_text: What percentage of your population is food insecure and/or lives in a food desert?
col1_Data availability: Data available for the percentage of population that is food insecure|Data available for the percentage of population that lives in a food desert
col4_Comment:
In 2013-2014, over 1 in 10 households (10.8%) were moderately or severely food insecure, nearly 1 in 10 children (9.7%) were moderately or severely food insecure and over 1 in 4 low-income households (27.4%) were moderately or severely food insecure. In addition, there is a map that highlights areas of Material Deprivation and Walkable Access to Grocery Stores for City of Windsor. Please refer to the map on page 137 (https://www.wechu.org/sites/default/files/create-resource/cdipplanningwindsorandessexcountycommunityfoodassessment2018final.pdf). 

News article from CBC states that there has been an 'increase of 61 per cent of Windsor-Essex residents visiting food banks from 2019 to 2022” (https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/windsor/windsor-food-banks-1.6632014). 

Data provided by the Windsor-Essex County Health Unit found that in Windsor and Essex County in 2021-2023, over 1 in 5 households (20.7%) faced food insecurity (https://www.wechu.org/food-and-nutrition/food-affordability). In 2023-2024, this grew to 25.7%. https://www.publichealthontario.ca/en/Data-and-Analysis/Health-Equity/Household-Food-Insecurity 

In Windsor-Essex, the weekly cost of groceries for a family of four in 2024 is $274.37. This works out to $1,188.01/month.

Despite these statistics, they are comparable to the provincial average. The Ontario average in fact is nearly 1 in 4 households experiencing some level of food insecurity in 2023. The average cost of groceries in the province of Ontario for a family of four is $1229. 

The City of Windsor is looking to improve these statistics by improving and expanding our community garden network, with a target focus on lower income, minority neighbourhoods. We currently have 10 community gardens with 161 beds for both community and private access, and this is continually being expanded with ongoing project proposals that are active right now (https://www.citywindsor.ca/residents/environment/community-gardens).

Em 2015-2016, dados da coorte EpiDoC (amostra representativa da população portuguesa) demonstravam que cerca de 19,3% dos agregados familiares portugueses encontravam-se numa situação de insegurança ou deserto alimentar, ou seja, numa situação em que se verificam dificuldades económicas no acesso aos alimentos (14,0% insegurança alimentar ligeira, 3,5% insegurança alimentar moderada e 1,8% insegurança alimentar grave/deserto alimentar) 
(https://nutrimento.pt/activeapp/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/PNPAS2022_2030_VF.pdf). 
Os valores agregados da população alvo de insegurança alimentar moderada e insegurança alimentar grave ou deserto alimentar totalizam uma percentagem de 5,3%. 
De acordo com uma publicação do Instituto Nacional de Estatística (INE) de abril deste ano (2025) no âmbito do Dia Mundial da Saúde, em 2024, 0.5% da população portuguesa encontrava-se em situação de insuficiência alimentar grave: 04DiaMSaúde_2025.pdf
Dados mais recentes apresentados na publicação nacional de acompanhamento estatístico da Agenda 2030 da ONU, intitulada “Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável: Indicadores para Portugal | Agenda 2030” mostram que há menor insegurança alimentar em Portugal, sendo realçada, pela positiva, a evolução da taxa de prevalência da insegurança alimentar moderada e/ou grave (taxa média de crescimento anual de -2,69% no período 2019-2024: ODS_20152024_PTa.pdf).
Este indicador considera a percentagem da população em risco moderado e severo de insegurança alimentar, não discriminando a percentagem da população em deserto alimentar.

The subsistence incidence rate in Davao City stands at 2.8% (PSA, 2021), equivalent to about 51.6 thousand individuals. Subsistence incidence is a poverty indicator that measures the proportion of the population living below the minimum income required to meet basic survival needs such as food, clothing, and shelter. While the percentage is relatively small compared to the total population of nearly 1.85 million, it highlights a vulnerable segment of society that continues to face challenges in meeting fundamental necessities. This emphasizes the need for targeted social protection and livelihood interventions to reduce inequality and uplift the most disadvantaged households.

On the other hand, approximately 25.01% of the population lives in food deserts, primarily in rural or geographically isolated barangays where access to grocery stores, supermarkets, and diverse food markets is limited. This condition underscores spatial inequalities in food access, which often contribute to higher living costs and reduced dietary diversity in these communities.

To address this, the recently approved Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) 2019-2028 integrates a Multinodal Concentric Spatial Strategy. This strategy is designed to improve the flow of farm inputs and services to production areas while enhancing the accessibility of crops, fruits, and other food products to nearby marketplaces. By strengthening connectivity and establishing nodes and districts as localized socio-economic centers, Davao City aims to bridge gaps in food distribution, improve food security, and ensure that even remote communities benefit from more affordable and nutritious food options.

Brighton and Hove City Council's food insecurity data is obtained from national and local datasets. The Food Foundation conduct regular nationally representative Food Insecurity Tracking surveys to assess UK food insecurity levels. From an online survey of 4028 adults in the United Kingdom commissioned by The Food Foundation and conducted between 29th January and 5th February 2025 by YouGov Plc (sixteenth in series) https://foodfoundation.org.uk/initiatives/food-insecurity-tracking.
7.3 million adults (13.9% of households) experienced food insecurity in January 2025; 2.4 million adults (4.6% of households) reported not eating for a whole day because they couldn't afford or get access to food; 17.9% of households with children reported that children were directly experiencing food insecurity; 38.7% of households in receipt of Universal Credit reported experiencing food insecurity; Non-white ethnic groups are at higher risk of food insecurity than white ethnic groups; Households with an adult limited a lot by disability are more likely to experience food insecurity than households with adult not limited by disability

Locally, the Brighton & Hove Food Partnership Emergency Food Network Survey 2024 asks a series of questions to organisations in Brighton and Hove providing food for people in financial insecurity. The survey is sent every July and asks projects to report on one week of activity Emergency Food Network Annual Report 2024 (bhfood.org.uk). Headline Stats - The Emergency Food Network now comprises 51 active member projects. Annual survey of food projects reveals 6,297 people need food support each week, with more than half seeking help on an ongoing basis. This is a similar number to the total beneficiaries supported in 2023, but still 18% higher than in 2022. 60 locations across all parts of the city offer food support. Projects are noticing an increase in the numbers of people with mental health issues, Black, Asian & Minoritised Ethnic people, and people in work seeking help. 
We also use the Consumer Data Research Centre's Priority Places for Food Index (PPFI rank) where a lower rank indicates higher food insecurity. 
Health Counts is a survey of Brighton & Hove residents conducted once a decade and is the largest health and wellbeing assessment in the city (16,729 people - 7.2% of the resident population aged 18 years or over). 40% reported spending less on food and 4% reported using support from charities (e.g. food banks) in 2024.

question_text: What percentage of your population is food insecure and/or lives in a food desert?
col1_Data availability: Data available for the percentage of population that is food insecure|Data available for the percentage of population that lives in a food desert
col4_Comment: The population % that is food insecure was assessed using a national study from the University of Sheffield in 2021. The study breaks down data for local authorities into the % of people who were 'hungry', 'struggling' and 'worried about' access to food. Those hungry include people who indicated that they were hungry but were unable to eat food because they could not afford it/were unable to access food in the previous month. Those struggling to access food include those who may have sought help within the last month with access to food, have cut back on meals to stretch tight budgets. Those who worry about food insecurity were people who were able to continue to supply food for their household, but may be just managing and could slip into food insecurity. As of Jan 2021, 3.23% of people were hungry, 9.83% were struggling and 13.60% were worried about food insecurity. Sunderland class people who are hungry/struggling as currently being in food insecurity and people who are worried as being at significant risk of slipping into food insecurity. The population % living in a food desert was calculated by working out how many households were outside of a 1-mile radius of a supermarket using UPRN data. The current cost of living crisis is increasing food insecurity in Sunderland. This is evidenced by the % of school children eligible for free school meals increasing by 12% from 2015/16-24/25, from 19.4% to 30.9%. While this is lower than the regional total of 32.3% for 24/25, it is higher than the 25.7% national total of children known to be eligible for free school meals. Sunderland Foodbank (SFB) consists of 11 sites across Sunderland. There are also around 50 independent food banks and crisis food providers that SCC provides financial and food support to, providing a range of support to people experiencing, or at risk of, food insecurity. According to SFB, the no. of people seeking food parcels decreased by 26% between 22/23-24/25 (13,120 to 9715). This is due to additional cost of living payments and household support fund payments. SCC also led the delivery of a Financial Wellbeing Strategy for Sunderland, working with partners across the city to reduce food poverty. SCC has partnered with 'The Bread and Butter Thing' charity, offering weekly groceries at a fraction of high street prices. Hubs are now in place in city-wide in Sunderland to ensure support is available across the city, serving 1000s each week. 2024 saw 18784 bags distributed (581177 meals).

col1_Data availability: Data available for the percentage of population that lives in a food desert|Data available for the percentage of population that is food insecure
col4_Comment:
1. Percentage of population facing food insecurity
The main causes of hunger in Taiwan are poverty, low income, and the limited mobility of elderly individuals living alone. Low-income households typically have low and unstable income, making it difficult to afford enough food. Elderly individuals living alone face hunger due to various reasons, including poor financial condition, lack of family support, lost contact with relatives, remote locations with limited access to food, or physical immobility and poor health that prevent them from preparing meals on their own. In the first quarter of 2025, there were approximately 36,336 individuals in the jurisdiction identified as low-income households or elderly individuals living alone, accounting for 0.89% of the total population. Considering the possible overlap with low-income households, persons with disabilities and homeless individuals were not included in the calculation.
*Elderly individuals living alone: Registered or actual residents of the city, aged 65 or above, living alone, and listed by the city government as care recipients after assessment.
*Low-income households: Registered or actual residents of the city, with an average monthly household income per person not exceeding NT$16,000, and total family-owned real estate not exceeding NT$4.2 million.

2. Percentage of population living in a food desert
The city is densely populated with hypermarkets, supermarkets, convenience stores, traditional markets, and night markets. According to real estate surveys, the four administrative districts with the highest supermarket density in Taiwan are all located in New Taipei City, namely Yonghe, Luzhou, Sanchong, and Banqiao. Yonghe District alone, with an area of just 5.71 square kilometers, has 30 supermarkets—equivalent to more than five supermarkets per square kilometer. The data reported in this questionnaire are based on the selection of 11 administrative districts—out of the city's total of 29 districts—that are located in mountainous or coastal areas and have relatively low population density, and the population of these districts was used for calculation.

Food insecurity and food deserts are terms that describe the challenges faced by populations in accessing essential food supplies. Food insecurity refers to the lack of regular access to sufficient, reliable, and nutritious food, while a food desert refers to areas, particularly in low-income neighborhoods, where fresh and healthy food options are scarce or unavailable.

The Beşiktaş district, being one of the more developed areas of Istanbul, generally does not experience significant issues in terms of food access. The district has numerous supermarkets, food markets, and local businesses that provide residents with a variety of food options, making food access relatively easier compared to other regions in Turkey. Additionally, due to the district's socioeconomic profile and its proximity to the city center, Beşiktaş enjoys advantages in terms of food availability.

However, the risk of food insecurity still exists, particularly for low-income households. Economic downturns, rising unemployment, or increasing energy costs may force some households to cut back on food expenditures. While comprehensive data specific to Beşiktaş is unavailable, it is important to note that urban areas with high living costs can place low-income individuals at a higher risk of food insecurity.

This aligns with the understanding that while Beşiktaş is not typically viewed as a high-risk area for food insecurity, there may still be underlying risks for certain vulnerable groups.

col4_Comment:
Em 2015-2016, dados da coorte EpiDoC (amostra representativa da população portuguesa) demonstravam que cerca de 19,3% dos agregados familiares portugueses encontravam-se numa situação de insegurança ou deserto alimentar, ou seja, numa situação em que se verificam dificuldades económicas no acesso aos alimentos (14,0% insegurança alimentar ligeira, 3,5% insegurança alimentar moderada e 1,8% insegurança alimentar grave/deserto alimentar) 
(https://nutrimento.pt/activeapp/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/PNPAS2022_2030_VF.pdf). 
Os valores agregados da população alvo de insegurança alimentar moderada e insegurança alimentar grave ou deserto alimentar totalizam uma percentagem de 5,3%. 
De acordo com uma publicação do Instituto Nacional de Estatística (INE) de abril deste ano (2025) no âmbito do Dia Mundial da Saúde, em 2024, 0.5% da população portuguesa encontrava-se em situação de insuficiência alimentar grave: 04DiaMSaúde_2025.pdf
Dados mais recentes apresentados na publicação nacional de acompanhamento estatístico da Agenda 2030 da ONU, intitulada “Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável: Indicadores para Portugal | Agenda 2030” mostram que há menor insegurança alimentar em Portugal, sendo realçada, pela positiva, a evolução da taxa de prevalência da insegurança alimentar moderada e/ou grave (taxa média de crescimento anual de -2,69% no período 2019-2024: ODS_20152024_PTa.pdf).
Este indicador considera a percentagem da população em risco moderado e severo de insegurança alimentar, não discriminando a percentagem da população em deserto alimentar.

1. Nutrition Plus Program
Nowon-gu implements the Nutrition Plus Program, a lifelong health management support service designed to improve the nutritional status of vulnerable groups and enhance their dietary management capacity. The program provides systematic nutrition education and essential nutrient-rich supplementary foods to pregnant women and young children at nutritional risk.

Target group: Infants and children under 6, pregnant women, postpartum women, and breastfeeding women residing in Nowon-gu, with household income at or below 80% of the national median income.

Support provided: Supply of supplementary foods such as powdered milk, rice, potatoes, carrots, eggs, milk, black beans, and chicken breast rice; along with tailored nutrition education and counseling services.

2. Agri-Food Voucher Program
To strengthen food access for vulnerable groups and build a sustainable agri-food consumption system that expands the national food security network, Nowon-gu is implementing the Agri-Food Voucher Program. This program provides eligible households with vouchers that can be used to purchase fresh domestic agricultural products.

Target group: Households receiving basic livelihood benefits (at or below 32% of the national median income) that include pregnant women, infants, or children under the age of 18.

Support provided: A monthly voucher (KRW 100,000 for a 4-person household) that can be used to purchase domestically produced fresh foods, including fruits, vegetables, white milk, fresh eggs, meat, grains, and tofu products (excluding processed foods).

Welsh Governments climate adaptation strategy published in 2024, sets out actions in relation to food security in the face of climate change. 
https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2024-10/climate-adaptation-strategy-for-wales-2024.pdf 

In 2018, Kellogg's commissioned an appraisal of 'food deserts' in the UK, defined as areas which are poorly served by food stores, particularly those selling fresh, healthy products. In these areas, where food choice is more limited than elsewhere, it may be particularly hard for households to buy healthy food conveniently, at a reasonable price. Food deserts may be especially challenging for those on low incomes, or vulnerable individuals such as those with a disability which limits their ability to travel. https://www.kelloggs.co.uk/content/dam/europe/kelloggs_gb/pdf/Kelloggs_Food_Desert_Brochure.pdf

9 areas in Wales were identified as being the most deprived 'food deserts' in Wales, with six of those areas being in the Cardiff Capital Region. An estimate of the population affected is around 15-20%.

col4_Comment: Food deserts are geographic areas where residents' access to healthy and affordable food is restricted or non-existent due to the absence or low density of “food entry points” within a practical travelling distance, defined by the USDA (2012) as a geographic area where at least 500 people or 33% of the population are located more than 1 mile (for urban areas) from the nearest supermarket or large grocery store. . The lack of access to healthy foods in these communities translates to health disparities and high rates of chronic disease. While we cannot provide the % residents in food deserts in the City, the E-food Desert Index shows the extent to which neighbourhoods exhibit characteristics associated with food deserts. It considers factors critical to measuring food deserts: Proximity and density of grocery retail facilities; Transport and accessibility; Neighbourhood socio-economic and demographic characteristics; E-commerce availability and propensity. The index identifies a new driver of inequalities in access to groceries - 'e-food deserts' - which are remoter parts of the capital that suffer comparatively poor access to both physical retail and limited provision of online grocery services. In this index (last updated in 2024), the City of London is not considered an e-food desert. The map produced by the index suggests that the City of London is ranking among the best in terms of food accessibility. Link: https://www.cdrc.ac.uk/ / https://data.cdrc.ac.uk/dataset/e-food-desert-index. While we cannot provide the % food insecure residents in the City, the London Resilience Strategy 2020 (https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/london_city_resilience_strategy_2020_digital.pdf) notes that 21% Londoners live in low or very low food security. The City differs significantly from the wider London area due to its unique demographic and economic profile, characterised by a high concentration of affluent businesses and relatively few residential areas, meaning it's anticipated that general London-wide statistics on food insecurity will not accurately reflect the specific needs and conditions of the Square Mile and is likely to be a much lower percentage.

The 2023 National Nutrition Survey (NNS) found that 31.4% of Filipino households faced moderate to severe food insecurity, with 2.7% experiencing severe insecurity. In Butuan City, family poverty incidence is 12.2%, slightly higher than the national average (10.9%) but lower than the Caraga regional average (20.3%). These numbers suggest that around 30-35% of Butuan's households, or 33,000-36,000 families, are food insecure. Additionally, some parts of the city are considered 'food insecure,' which have limited or uncertain access to enough safe and nutritious food. 

To address these concerns, Butuan City has integrated sustainable and green investments into its agricultural and fisheries programs. The Organic Agriculture Program aims to convert at least 436 hectares (5% of farmland) into certified organic areas, with transitional support for farmers to mitigate income losses during the shift from conventional practices. Complementing this effort, the Butuan City Rice Research Center (BCRRC) in Brgy. Los Angeles establishes 19 hectares of demonstration plots for rice variety testing and the promotion of organic rice protocols. 

Further diversification is evident in the Integrated Diversified Organic and Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) Farms in Brgy. Pigdaulan, which operate an organic demonstration farm, a GAP-certified farm, and a plant nursery producing vermicompost, fruit trees, and vegetable seedlings. Fisheries-based sustainability is pursued through FishCORE, a BFAR-initiated project, which strengthens coastal resource management, supports alternative livelihoods (aquaculture and post-harvest processing), and rehabilitates ecosystems such as mangroves and coral reefs. In parallel, the Gulayan sa Komunidad initiative promotes community-based vegetable production, enhancing household-level food security. These initiatives are reinforced by AgriBOOST, Butuan's flagship program that has increased local vegetable production by 88% and processing volume by 52% (2024), reducing dependence on imported supply. 

The city's integration of organic agriculture, rice research, diversified farms, fisheries management, and community gardens represents a holistic response linking food security with environmental sustainability. If sustained, these investments can reduce food insecurity by an estimated 5-7 percentage points in two (2) years, while positioning Butuan City as a model for climate-resilient and nutrition-sensitive urban governance.

En el municipio Maneiro, al igual que en gran parte de la Isla de Margarita, la inseguridad alimentaria se encuentra estrechamente vinculada a la precariedad en los servicios básicos, la dependencia de importaciones y las limitaciones propias de un territorio insular sin fuentes locales de producción sostenida. Aunque el 96,27% de las viviendas cuenta con acceso a agua por tuberías, la inestabilidad del servicio, la irregularidad en los ciclos de distribución y la necesidad de recurrir a cisternas encarecen la vida diaria y limitan la preparación adecuada y segura de alimentos. Estos problemas en el acceso al agua, sumados a los altos costos de transporte y almacenamiento de productos, agravan la vulnerabilidad nutricional de la población.

La condición de “desierto alimentario” se hace evidente en sectores donde la oferta de alimentos frescos es limitada y costosa, predominando el acceso a productos procesados de baja calidad nutricional. El abastecimiento depende en gran medida del ingreso irregular de productos desde tierra firme, sujetos a interrupciones en la cadena logística y a incrementos constantes de precios. La capacidad adquisitiva de la población, afectada por salarios muy por debajo del costo de la canasta alimentaria, restringe el acceso a dietas balanceadas, lo que incrementa la dependencia de carbohidratos y alimentos de bajo valor nutritivo.

En las comunidades más vulnerables del municipio, las familias priorizan la cantidad sobre la calidad de los alimentos, lo que se traduce en deficiencias de proteínas, frutas y vegetales. Estos patrones de consumo, agravados por los altos niveles de subempleo, impactan directamente en la salud pública y en la capacidad de los hogares para enfrentar riesgos climáticos, ya que la malnutrición reduce la resiliencia individual y comunitaria.

En síntesis, una proporción significativa de la población de Maneiro enfrenta inseguridad alimentaria, y varios sectores urbanos y periurbanos pueden clasificarse como desiertos alimentarios por la falta de acceso asequible y regular a alimentos nutritivos. Esta situación compromete tanto la calidad de vida de los habitantes como las perspectivas de desarrollo económico y social del municipio.

col1_Data availability: Data available for the percentage of population that is food insecure
col4_Comment:
A estimativa de 37% de população com insegurança alimentar em Vitória de Santo Antão (PE) usa um proxy robusto baseado nas fontes oficiais e reconhecidas no país. A PNAD Contínua - Suplemento de Segurança Alimentar 2023 (IBGE) reporta que 35,0% da população do Nordeste vive em algum grau de insegurança alimentar (leve, moderada ou grave). Em municípios de porte e perfil socioeconômico semelhantes ao de Vitória, a literatura e séries históricas com a EBIA indicam taxas ligeiramente superiores à média regional; por isso, adotamos 37% como ponto central, refletindo a vulnerabilidade local (renda, informalidade e acesso a serviços). Essa é uma estimativa conservadora e justificável para reporte ao CDP quando não há mensuração direta municipal recente.
	•	PNAD Contínua 2023 - Segurança Alimentar (IBGE):
https://biblioteca.ibge.gov.br/visualizacao/livros/liv102079.pdf
	•	II Inquérito Nacional sobre Insegurança Alimentar no Brasil 2022 (Rede PENSSAN):
https://olheparaafome.com.br
	•	Atlas da Insegurança Alimentar nos Municípios Brasileiros 2023 (IPEA):
https://www.ipea.gov.br/atlasinsegalimentar/

Como ler o número: “37%” significa que cerca de 37 em cada 100 moradores podem enfrentar restrições no acesso regular e adequado a alimentos ao longo do ano. No contexto municipal, isso se manifesta por intermitência de renda, preços elevados de alimentos básicos, variações climáticas (estiagem/enchentes) que afetam produção e abastecimento, e custos de energia que competem com o orçamento doméstico.

Por que usar este proxy no CDP: (1) O IBGE é a fonte oficial mais atual e comparável para segurança/insegurança alimentar; (2) a PENSSAN complementa a leitura com foco em vulnerabilidades graves; (3) o IPEA oferece visão territorializada e insumos para calibrar a realidade municipal. Na ausência de um inquérito EBIA amostral específico para Vitória de Santo Antão em 2023-2024, o uso da taxa regional (35%) com ajuste técnico para 37% é metodologicamente defensável e evita subestimação.

Nota para o portal do CDP: indicar no campo “Explain” que o valor municipal foi estimado a partir da PNAD Contínua 2023 - Nordeste, com ajuste por vulnerabilidade local com base em evidências (PENSSAN e Atlas IPEA), e que o município pretende realizar medição direta (inquérito EBIA local) em cooperação com a Saúde/Assistência Social para aprimorar o indicador nos próximos ciclos.

col4_Comment:
The Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) of Balanga City provides insight into the socioeconomic vulnerabilities that directly link to food insecurity. According to the assessment, the city's poverty incidence is 4.4%, significantly lower than the provincial average of Bataan and the national average. This means that approximately 4,824 individuals out of the city's 109,647 population (2023 baseline) live below the poverty threshold.

Using the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) benchmarks from FAO and national surveys, it is recognized that food insecurity extends beyond official poverty incidence. Nationally, 31% of households are moderately to severely food insecure, while in urbanized centers with better market access like Balanga, the adjusted estimate ranges between 20-25% of the population. Applying this range to Balanga yields an estimated 21,900-27,400 individuals who are food insecure despite relatively low poverty incidence.

The CDRA also reports malnutrition indicators, with childhood stunting at 12.6% and underweight prevalence at 8.1%, reflecting nutritional deficiencies that correlate with food insecurity. These nutrition outcomes highlight that even with good physical access to food markets in Balanga, dietary quality and affordability remain challenges, particularly for vulnerable households.

From a spatial perspective, while Balanga's urban core is well-served by public markets and commercial centers, peripheral barangays — particularly upland and coastal areas — have more limited and irregular access to affordable, nutritious food. It is estimated that 5-7% of the city's population live in such food desert-like conditions, representing around 5,500-7,700 individuals.

col4_Comment: El porcentaje de población con inseguridad alimentaria indicado: 15,7 (con un márgen de error de ±1,1 para un nivel de confianza del 95%); corresponde al resultado, para inseguridad alimentaria moderada y grave en Canelones, de un estudio incluido en la encuesta continua de hogares (ECH) del Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE) en 2022.Hasta el año pasado, Canelones y el país no disponían de estadísticas oficiales sobre la prevalencia de inseguridad alimentaria. Únicamente existían reportes de diversos estudios realizados en poblaciones específicas. El INE realizó la encuesta como un módulo de preguntas extras en el cuestionario de la ECH.Se utilizó la Escala FIES, desarrollada por la FAO como el instrumento de referencia para la medida de la inseguridad alimentaria. Para el análisis, se utilizó un modelo de Rasch, ya que permite estimar la probabilidad de que una persona haya experimentado inseguridad alimentaria a partir de su patrón de respuestas a las preguntas de la escala FIES. El modelo presentó un ajuste adecuado a los datos. El modelo de Rasch permite ordenar las preguntas de la escala según la severidad de la experiencia de inseguridad alimentaria que representan y en este estudio se siguieron los criterios de la FAO. Para la estimación de la inseguridad alimentaria moderada o grave se consideró la pregunta con menor seveSe indica que el 0.0% de la población vive en un desierto alimentario, debido a que se entiende que en Canelones no existen áreas geográficas donde el acceso de los residentes a los alimentos sea limitado o nulo debido a la ausencia o baja densidad de “puntos de ingreso de alimentos” a una distancia de traslado práctica según los criterios de la FAO. Tampoco áreas geográficas donde al menos 500 personas o el 33 % de la población está ubicada a más de 1 milla (áreas urbanas) o 10 millas (áreas rurales) del supermercado o la tienda de alimentos más cercana, de acuerdo a los criterios de USDA.
